item.description:
⌘T goes where you meant, open or not

The ⌘T panel has a name now: Navigator. In 0.4 it found the tabs you already had open. Now it covers the rest of what ⌘T is for. Type a few letters of a site and the page you visit most that starts with them is the top row, so you goes to youtube.com. Anything that isn't an address is a web search. Your history is ranked by how often and how recently you visited each page, across every profile, and fuzzy matches against open tabs sit below that.

The search uses the browser's own engine, read from the profile (in Safari, its own “search the web”). To use one engine in every browser, pick it in “Searches with” under the ⌘T switch in the rules window, or add a search template line to the rules file.

  • The row under the cursor says where ↩ goes: “Go to youtube.com”, or “Search google.com”.
  • Nothing is selected until you type or press ↓, so ↩ on an empty panel still opens a new tab the way it always did.
  • Rows appear at once from the last list Navigator read, and the list is refreshed behind them.
  • Navigator hides when you switch to another app or click outside it.
  • Pasting a paragraph gives you one search: line breaks become spaces, and the field stays one line that scrolls sideways.
  • Type settings to open the BrowserRouter rules window without reaching for the mouse.
  • Titles and addresses now line up on one line, and shortcut keys sit in square keycaps.
  • The rules file still calls it tabswitcher, so existing rules keep working.

Click the same link twice and it opens in a browser

A rule that sends a link to an app is a standing guess about where that link belongs, and until now the only way past a wrong guess was opening the editor. The second click is the moment you can say not that one: click the same link again within four seconds and every app rule is skipped, so it falls through to whichever browser would otherwise have had it.

Nothing else changes. The rules are untouched, the app rule is still there for the next link, and the same click delivered twice — which macOS does now and then — is not read as a correction.

  • The checkbox is under “Everything else” in the rules window, and it is on by default: it costs nothing until a link is deliberately clicked twice.
  • In the rules file it is a secondclick browser line, and secondclick off turns it off.
  • BrowserRouter --route ignores it, so a script routing the same url in a loop still answers the same way every time.

Rules are a list you order, and deep links are something you can read

The first rule that matches now wins, so the order of the list is what decides. New rules are placed narrowest first, so a broad one added later does not quietly shadow a narrow one that was already there — and the arrows under the table are how you overrule that when you want to.

The nine app handoffs are ordinary rules now. They used to be checkboxes, which said the list of apps was nine long. Each one is a line in the table you can read, move, edit or delete, and writing your own takes nothing special:

app:bear://{rest}    link    bear.app/{rest...}

Deep links are a pattern and a template. zoom.us/j/{id} becomes zoommtg://{host}/join?confno={id}, written in the rules file rather than compiled into the app. The vocabulary is four things: {name} for one path segment, {name...} for the rest of the url, {host} for the host that matched, and ?key={name} for a query parameter found wherever it actually appears. A pattern that does not match is an app declining the link, so zoom.us/pricing goes to a browser without anything being written to say so.

  • Rules can be edited, not only added and deleted.
  • Presets moved into the add button, next to “New rule…”.
  • BrowserRouter --save rewrites the rules file in the current format.
  • The rules file documents the whole vocabulary, so anything that can write a line of text can add a rule.
